fetched_contents.text: Discrete cosine transform Technique used in signal processing and data compression A discrete cosine transform (DCT) expresses a finite sequence of data points in terms of a sum of cosine functions oscillating at different frequencies. The DCT, first proposed by Nasir Ahmed in 1972, is a widely used transformation technique in signal processing and data compression. It is used in most digital media, including digital images (such as JPEG and HEIF), digital video (such as MPEG and H.26x), digital audio (such as Dolby Digital, MP3 and AAC), digital television (such as SDTV, HDTV and VOD), digital radio (such as AAC+ and DAB+), and speech coding (such as AAC-LD, Siren and Opus). DCTs are also important to numerous other applications in science and engineering, such as digital signal processing, telecommunication devices, reducing network bandwidth usage, and spectral methods for the numerical solution of partial differential equations. A DCT is a Fourier-related transform similar to the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), but using only real numbers. The DCTs are generally related to Fourier series coefficients of a periodically and symmetrically extended sequence whereas DFTs are related to Fourier series coefficients of only periodically extended sequences. DCTs are equivalent to DFTs of roughly twice the length, operating on real data with even symmetry (since the Fourier transform of a real and even function is real and even), whereas in some variants the input or output data are shifted by half a sample. From the perspective of algebraic signal processing, the relationship between the DCT and the DFT reflects their different underlying algebraic structures: the DFT basis functions are the irreducible representations of the cyclic group, making the DFT the natural spectral transform for signals with periodic (circular) boundary conditions, while the DCT basis functions are the irreducible representations of the dihedral group, making the DCT natural for signals with symmetric (even) boundary conditions.[1] There are eight standard DCT variants, of which four are common. The most common variant of discrete cosine transform is the type-II DCT, which is often called simply the DCT. This was the original DCT as first proposed by Ahmed. Its inverse, the type-III DCT, is correspondingly often called simply the inverse DCT or the IDCT. Two related transforms are the discrete sine transform (DST), which is equivalent to a DFT of real and odd functions, and the modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT), which is based on a DCT of overlapping data. Multidimensional DCTs (MD DCTs) are developed to extend the concept of DCT to multidimensional signals. A variety of fast algorithms have been developed to reduce the computational complexity of implementing DCT. One of these is the integer DCT (IntDCT),[2] an integer approximation of the standard DCT,[3]: ix, xiii, 1, 141–304 used in several ISO/IEC and ITU-T international standards.[2][3] DCT compression, also known as block compression, compresses data in sets of discrete DCT blocks.[4] DCT blocks sizes including 8 × 8 pixels for the standard DCT, and varied integer DCT sizes between 4 × 4 and 32 × 32 pixels.[2][5] The DCT has a strong energy compaction property,[6][7] capable of achieving high quality at high data compression ratios.[8][9] However, blocky compression artifacts can appear when heavy DCT compression is applied. History The DCT was first conceived by Nasir Ahmed while working at Kansas State University. The concept was proposed to the National Science Foundation in 1972. The DCT was originally intended for image compression.[10][2] Ahmed developed a practical DCT algorithm with his PhD students T. Raj Natarajan and K. R. Rao at the University of Texas at Arlington in 1973.[10] They presented their results in a January 1974 paper, titled Discrete Cosine Transform.[6][7][11] It described what is now called the type-II DCT (DCT-II),[3]: 51 as well as the type-III inverse DCT (IDCT).[6] Since its introduction in 1974, there has been significant research on the DCT.[11] In 1977, Wen-Hsiung Chen published a paper with C. Harrison Smith and Stanley C. Fralick presenting a fast DCT algorithm.[12][11] Further developments include a 1978 paper by M. J. Narasimha and A. M. Peterson, and a 1984 paper by B. G. Lee.[11] These research papers, along with the original 1974 Ahmed paper and the 1977 Chen paper, were cited by the Joint Photographic Experts Group as the basis for JPEG's lossy image compression algorithm in 1992.[11][13] The discrete sine transform (DST) was derived from the DCT, by replacing the Neumann condition at x=0 with a Dirichlet condition.[3]: 35-36 The DST was described in the 1974 DCT paper by Ahmed, Natarajan and Rao.[6] A type-I DST (DST-I) was later described by Anil K. Robinson adapted the DCT for inter-frame motion-compensated video coding. They experimented with the DCT and the fast Fourier transform (FFT), developing inter-frame hybrid coders for both, and found that the DCT is the most efficient due to its reduced complexity, capable of compressing image data down to 0.25-bit per pixel for a videotelephone scene with image quality comparable to an intra-frame coder requiring 2-bit per pixel.[15][16] In 1979, Anil K. fetched_contents.text: Analysis of DWT–DCT watermarking algorithm on digital medical imaging Abstract. Purpose Over the past decade, the diagnostic information of the patients are digitally recorded and transferred. During the transmission of patients data, the security and authenticity of the information has to be ensured. Medical image watermarking technology has recently advanced because it can be used to conceal patient information while ensuring the authenticity. We propose a multiple watermarking method for securing clinical medical images. Approach In this watermarking method, the quality feature property and private label property information are embedded as watermarks in the original image. Initially, medical images are divided into the region of interest (ROI) and non-interest region (NIR). Second, a two-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is applied to the ROI and the coefficients LL1 (LL2, LH2, HL2, HH2), LH1, HL1, and HH1 are generated. Watermarks are embedded using the DWT low-frequency sub-band (LL2) by quantizing the low-frequency coefficients. Next, the NIR is separated into non-overlapping 8×8 blocks, and a discrete cosine transform (DCT) is applied for each block. The DCT coefficients of each block are sorted using the zigzag transform. For embedding, eight intermediate frequency coefficients are used. Finally, the feature information is embedded in the ROI, and the tag information is embedded in the NIR. Results The performance of the DWT-DCT watermarking method is calculated using the metrics of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure, and mean square error. The proposed method obtained the better PSNR value of 45.76 dB. Conclusions The proposed model works well for clinical medical images when compared with the existing techniques. Keywords: medical image, multiple watermarks, quantization, region of interest, non-interest region, discrete wavelet transform, discrete cosine transform, zigzag sort, Arnold transform, logistic encryption, peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index measure, mean square error 1. Introduction Since the advent of the Internet, a new field known as telemedicine has emerged; it has made access to healthcare and accessibility of records easier. Hospitals in many countries use electronic patient records to maintain patients’ medical data (diseases name, disease size, disease affected area, etc.), private data (name, birth date, gender, address, etc.), and financial data (payment by cash/debit card/credit card/UPI), and these can be transferred to any corner of the world with accessibility to the Internet.1 But the data may get tampered with unintentionally or intentionally while being transferred. To prevent a misdiagnosis, sensitive, private, and useful information can be encrypted and embedded into it in the form of a watermark. This would serve as a medium not only of authentication but also of integrity.2,3 In recent years, a significant amount of work has been carried out for watermarking algorithms in medical images. In 2004, Nayak et al.4 developed a watermarking algorithm with embedding and encryption techniques. In 2006, Trichili et al.5 presented the watermarking embedding algorithm with encryption and decryption methods to secure the patient information. In 2007, Zian et al.6 introduced the reversible watermarking approach for embedding the secure patient information. In 2011, Osamah et al.7 used the fragile watermarking technique to embed the patient’s information in the transform domain. In 2010, Salwa et al.8 developed the watermarking algorithm using a wavelet based data embedding approach. In 2015, Lu et al.1 proposed the multiple watermarking scheme that used the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and discrete cosine transform (DCT) techniques. In 2017, Natu et al.9 combined singular vector decomposition (SVD) and DCT to embed the patient information in the cover image. fetched_contents.text: Robust and blind image watermarking in DCT domain using inter-block coefficient correlation Abstract This study presents a robust and transparent watermarking method that exploits block-based discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficient modification. The difference in the DCT coefficients of two blocks is calculated and modified based on the watermark bit to adjust this difference to a predefined range. The first coefficient in the upper left corner of the array basis function is known as the direct current (DC) coefficient, whereas the remainder includes the alternating current (AC) coefficients. The extent of the DCT coefficient modifications depends on the DC coefficient and median of the AC coefficients ordered by a zig-zag sequence. The robustness of the proposed method against various attacks was evaluated experimentally, and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method possesses great robustness against various single and combined attacks. Introduction Copyright violations have increased owing to the recent advancements in Internet technologies. Digital property can be easily distributed globally. Consequently, digital image watermarking is used to prevent the copyright violations. Watermarking involves embedding information to protect the ownership and integrity of the digital content. Watermarked content is nearly the same as the original content, and digital watermarks are difficult to detect and remove without damaging the original content. A content owner can embed the ownership information into digital content, such as images [10], video [4], and audio [8], using a digital watermark. Effective watermarks should be robust against alterations and imperceptibility [15]. Watermarking techniques involve spatial and transform domains. In the spatial domain, a watermark is embedded in an image by directly modifying the pixels [12], [18], whereas in the transform domain, watermark is embedded by modifying the coefficients of the transformed image [16], [17]. Spatial domain techniques have lower computational complexity than the transformed domain techniques but tend to be less robust. On the contrary, the transformed domain techniques feature higher computational complexity with greater robustness. Herein, we focus on a transform domain watermarking scheme. Several transform techniques, such as Fourier transform (FT), discrete wavelet transform (DWT) [6], [19], singular value decomposition (SVD) [1], [3], [9], and discrete cosine transform (DCT), have been proposed. There are several types of FT, such as discrete FT, fast FT, fractional FT [11], and quaternion FT [20]. FT is robust against common image attacks but not against geometric attacks, such as JPEG compression and rotation. DWT is used for JPEG2000 and requires more transformation time than DCT. The SVD method is a matrix factorization that can be designed as a reversible watermarking technique. However, SVD is more complex than DCT and DWT; therefore, it is not suitable for software and hardware implementations in low-cost devices, thereby making DCT popular in the transform domain [7], [13], [14]. DCT can be computed on the entire image or non-overlapping blocks of a specified size. After DCT is performed, a block can be separated into low, middle, and high frequency subband coefficients. Coefficients changed in the high frequency subband will not significantly degrade image quality. On the contrary, the low frequency subband comprises most of the image and any change in this subband will change the image quality significantly. To obtain a high quality and robust watermarked image, middle frequency subband coefficients are most suitable for embedding watermark bits. Recently, several watermarking methods have been developed. Golabi et al. [5] proposed a watermarking method based on the features of radical moment. This method is robust against rotation and scaling attacks. However, moment-based techniques are not robust against cropping attacks. Furthermore, the total watermark bits can be embedded into a 512 × 512 cover image only 127 bits. Patra et al. [14] proposed a DCT watermarking scheme based on Chinese remainder theorem (CRT). In the scheme, the host image is divided into 8 × 8 pixel blocks, a block is selected, and DCT is applied randomly. Then, a watermark bit and DCT coefficient are selected, and CRT is used to calculate the amount of modification based on several conditions. This scheme has low computational complexity and is robust against common image processing attacks. This scheme is robust against 10% cropping attacks; however, it has not been tested against 25% cropping attacks. Das et al. [2] proposed a watermarking scheme based on the inter-block coefficient correlation in DCT. They only changed one coefficient in each block based on the predefined threshold. This scheme is robust against JPEG compression and common image attacks with the watermark logo being restricted to 64 × 63 pixels for a 512 × 512 cover image because some blocks on the border cannot be used for embedding. Parah et al. [13] proposed a watermarking scheme based on inter-block coefficient differencing in DCT. They considered all blocks and made use of the coefficient differences for embedding. This scheme can use 64 × 64 watermark for 512 × 512 image and is robust against various attacks. However, it does not consider the correlation between upper and lower blocks and the quantized factor is fixed to each block coefficient. Consequently, the scheme would be vulnerable to multiple attacks. Branch report on the embedding workflow

DCT-based watermark embedding follows a structured workflow that begins with image preprocessing and ends with inverse DCT reconstruction of the watermarked image. The evidence shows that the host image is typically divided into blocks, then transformed with DCT, and the watermark is embedded in selected frequency coefficients before reconstruction [N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-F2]. The workflow described in the DWT–DCT medical-image study gives a concrete example: the image is divided into non-overlapping 8×8 blocks, DCT is applied to each block, and the coefficients are sorted using a zigzag transform before watermark embedding [N2-F2]. That same source also states that inverse DCT is applied to reconstruct the watermarked image, which means the process is a closed loop of transformation, modification, and synthesis [N2-F2].

For image preprocessing, the main steps are block partitioning and DCT transformation. The evidence repeatedly points to 8×8 blocks as a common partitioning choice. One source explicitly says the host image is divided into 16×16 non-overlapping blocks that undergo the DCT transform, and each 16×16 DCT block is further decomposed into four 8×8 sub-blocks [N6-R1]. Another source says the image is broken into 8×8 blocks of pixels and DCT is applied to each block [N6-R4]. The DWT–DCT medical-image study also divides the image into non-overlapping 8×8 blocks and applies DCT to each block [N2-F2]. This suggests that block size and partitioning are highly practical choices in DCT watermarking, often implemented as 8×8 blocks or larger blocks subdivided into smaller sub-blocks.

Watermark generation and normalization are central to embedding strength control. The evidence indicates that watermark bits are extracted from the 8×8 sub-blocks or from the blocks themselves, and normalization is used to prepare the watermark for embedding [N2-F2][N6-R2]. A separate source notes that normalization and quantization are important in quantization-based watermarking [N5-R2]. More generally, watermarking implementations often normalize the watermark signal to a small range, which is a key step for controlling how much the coefficients are modified. The DWT–DCT study shows that the watermark is embedded using the DCT coefficients of each block after sorting, and the embedding process modifies the coefficients before inverse DCT reconstruction [N2-F2]. The normalization step is therefore essential because it scales the watermark to a level compatible with the host signal and avoids distortion.

Coefficient modification is the core embedding operation. The evidence states that watermark bits are embedded by modifying the DCT coefficients, and the extent of modification depends on the DC coefficient and the median of the ordered AC coefficients [N3-F3]. In other words, the watermark is inserted into selected frequency coefficients, not uniformly across all coefficients. The same source explains that the first coefficient in the upper left corner of the block is the DC coefficient, while the rest are AC coefficients [N3-F3]. It also says that changes in the high-frequency subband do not significantly degrade image quality, while changes in the low-frequency subband can change image quality significantly [N3-F3]. The practical implication is that watermark embedding is typically done in the middle or high-frequency regions, where the perceptual impact is smaller and the robustness to attacks is better [N3-F3].

Inverse DCT reconstruction completes the embedding process. The DWT–DCT medical-image study explicitly says that inverse DCT is applied to reconstruct the watermarked image [N2-F2]. This means that after the watermark is embedded into the selected DCT coefficients, the modified block is transformed back to the spatial domain to produce the final watermarked image. The evidence also shows that watermarking methods may use multiple blocks and coefficient-level operations, such as inter-block coefficient correlation or differencing, to adjust the modification amount [N3-F3]. This implies that the reconstruction phase is not merely a simple inverse transform; it may involve careful synthesis of modified coefficients across blocks, especially when robustness and transparency are jointly optimized [N3-F3].

Overall, the embedding workflow is: image partitioning → DCT transformation → watermark normalization and generation → coefficient modification → inverse DCT reconstruction. The evidence supports a clear sequence in which preprocessing and transformation are followed by watermark insertion and final synthesis, with block size, normalization, and coefficient selection being the main practical controls [N2-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R4].

In DCT-based watermarking, coefficient selection is the key decision that balances imperceptibility and robustness. The evidence shows that watermarking methods often choose a subset of coefficients rather than modifying all coefficients indiscriminately. One source explicitly states that watermark bits are embedded by modifying the DCT coefficients of each block, and the difference in the DCT coefficients of two blocks is calculated and modified based on the watermark bit [N3-F3]. This indicates that watermarking is not a global modification of the entire block; instead, selected coefficients are adjusted in a way that depends on the block structure.

The evidence also identifies DC and AC coefficients as the main categories of DCT coefficients. The source explains that the first coefficient in the upper left corner is the DC coefficient, and the remainder are AC coefficients [N3-F3]. This distinction matters because DC coefficients represent the overall energy of the block, while AC coefficients capture the finer frequency details. The same source notes that changes in the high-frequency subband do not significantly degrade image quality, whereas changes in the low-frequency subband can change image quality significantly [N3-F3]. Therefore, watermark embedding is often done in the middle or high-frequency regions, where the perceptual impact is smaller and the robustness to attacks is better. The source also says that middle frequency subband coefficients are most suitable for embedding watermark bits, which is a direct statement of the coefficient-selection rationale [N3-F3].

How embedding strength is controlled is closely tied to the selection of coefficients and the amount of modification. The evidence shows that the extent of modification depends on the DC coefficient and the median of the ordered AC coefficients [N3-F3]. This is a form of adaptive embedding: the watermark is inserted more conservatively when the host block has a higher DC coefficient or when the AC coefficients are larger, which helps preserve image quality. Another source on quantization-based watermarking emphasizes normalization and quantization as important practical tools for controlling embedding strength [N5-R2]. The DWT–DCT medical-image study also discusses normalization and quantization in the context of watermark embedding, though the exact normalization method is not specified in the excerpt [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that embedding strength is controlled by normalizing the watermark, quantizing it, and adjusting the modification amount relative to the host block’s DCT structure.

The tradeoffs between imperceptibility and robustness are a major theme in the evidence. The source on robust and blind watermarking in the DCT domain says that robustness and transparency are always a trade-off in digital watermarking methods [N3-F3]. Another source notes that DCT is popular in the transform domain because it is more suitable for software and hardware implementations in low-cost devices than SVD [N3-F3]. This is relevant because lower computational complexity can make watermarking more practical, but it does not automatically mean higher robustness. The evidence also shows that some methods trade off robustness against different attacks by choosing different coefficient regions: for example, high-frequency regions are less perceptible but may be less robust, while middle-frequency regions are a compromise [N3-F3]. The same source says that robust watermarking methods can be made more transparent by considering the likely set of attacks, which means that robustness is not a fixed property but depends on the attack model [N4-R3]. The evidence further indicates that watermarking schemes can be robust against JPEG compression and common image attacks, but they may still be vulnerable to multiple attacks if not carefully designed [N3-F3].

In practical terms, the tradeoff is managed by selecting the right coefficients, controlling the embedding strength through normalization and quantization, and choosing a block structure that supports both transparency and robustness. The evidence supports the conclusion that DCT watermarking is often used in the middle or high-frequency regions because these regions allow watermark insertion without severe visual distortion, while still providing reasonable robustness against common attacks [N3-F3][N4-R3]. At the same time, the same evidence shows that stronger embedding can increase robustness at the cost of greater perceptibility, which is why watermarking is inherently a balancing act [N3-F3][N4-R3].

The same source notes that the DCT is often used in lossy compression, which is directly relevant to watermarking because watermarking often involves modifying the host signal in a way that is imperceptible but detectable [N1-F1].

DCT is suitable for watermarking because it provides a compact representation of the host image in terms of frequency coefficients. The evidence states that DCT compression compresses data in sets of discrete DCT blocks, and that DCT blocks sizes including 8×8 pixels are common [N1-F1]. The DCT-based watermarking rationale therefore lies in the fact that the image can be represented as a set of coefficients that can be modified without drastically altering the visual appearance of the host image. The source also says that the DCT has a strong energy compaction property, capable of achieving high quality at high data compression ratios [N1-F1]. This is important because watermarking modifies only a small portion of the coefficients, preserving the overall image structure while embedding hidden information.

The evidence explains how DCT partitions the image into frequency coefficients. This means that the DCT divides the image into small blocks, each of which is then represented as a set of frequency coefficients, and those coefficients are often ordered by frequency content using a zigzag pattern [N2-F2][N3-R4].

The rationale for watermarking using DCT is therefore built on three main properties: energy compaction, compact block representation, and the ability to modify selected coefficients without large visual changes. The evidence states that changes in the high-frequency subband do not significantly degrade image quality, whereas changes in the low-frequency subband can change image quality significantly [N3-F3]. This means that watermark embedding is typically done in the middle or high-frequency regions, where the perceptual impact is smaller and the robustness to attacks is better. The low-frequency region is avoided or used sparingly because modifying it can visibly alter the image [N3-F3]. The source also notes that the DC coefficient is the first coefficient in the upper left corner, and the rest are AC coefficients, which reinforces the idea that watermarking is often done in the AC region rather than the DC region [N3-F3].

In summary, DCT is suitable for watermarking because it provides a compact frequency representation with strong energy compaction, and it partitions the image into blocks and frequency coefficients that can be modified selectively. Low-frequency regions are treated carefully because changes there can degrade image quality, while high- and middle-frequency regions are preferred for watermarking because they allow robust embedding with less perceptible distortion [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R4].

## Integrated explanation of DCT-based watermark embedding

DCT-based watermark embedding is a transform-domain method in which a watermark is inserted into a host image by modifying selected frequency coefficients in the DCT domain. The main idea is that the DCT provides a compact and structured representation of the image, making it possible to embed hidden information in a way that is imperceptible to the human eye while remaining robust to common image manipulations. The evidence shows that DCT is used because it has strong energy compaction, can represent images in blocks of coefficients, and is computationally manageable for many watermarking applications [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R4].

## 1) Why DCT is used for watermarking

The discrete cosine transform (DCT) is a frequency-domain transformation that expresses a finite sequence of data points as a sum of cosine functions oscillating at different frequencies [N1-F1]. It is especially useful in signal and image processing because it has strong energy compaction properties, meaning most of the signal energy is concentrated in a small number of coefficients [N1-F1][N3-F3]. This makes the DCT a good choice for watermarking because it allows the host image to be represented in a way that is both compact and structured, so that watermarking can be done without drastically altering the overall image appearance.

The evidence also emphasizes that DCT compression compresses data in sets of discrete DCT blocks, and that DCT block sizes include 8×8 pixels and other sizes [N1-F1]. This means the DCT naturally partitions the image into blocks, which is important for watermarking because it allows the image to be processed in manageable pieces rather than as a single large matrix. The same source notes that the DCT is widely used in digital media and data compression, including JPEG and HEIF images, because of its strong energy compaction property [N1-F1].
